drills.q: What does DFS's recursion depth actually correspond to -- total nodes, or something else?
drills.a: The height of the tree, or more generally the longest path DFS descends before backtracking -- not the total node count. A balanced tree of a million nodes recurses only about 20 levels deep; a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) tree of the same size recurses a million levels deep.

drills.q: In iterative preorder DFS with an explicit stack, why must the right child be pushed before the left child?
drills.a: A stack is LIFO, so whatever is pushed last is popped first. Pushing right first means left ends up on top of the stack and gets popped and visited before right, matching the expected left-before-right preorder sequence.

drills.q: Explain precisely what changes and what does NOT change when you convert a recursive DFS to an iterative one with an explicit stack.
drills.a: What does NOT change: the asymptotic auxiliary space complexity, which remains O(H) in both forms (H being the maximum depth/height reached). What DOES change: which physical memory resource holds that O(H) footprint -- recursive DFS consumes call-stack memory, a small and fixed-size resource per thread (commonly a low single-digit number of megabytes, translating to roughly a thousand to a few tens of thousands of frames before overflow, and specifically about 1000 frames by default in Python regardless of available RAM); iterative DFS consumes heap memory, which is typically far larger and can grow until the process exhausts available RAM. The conversion trades a small hard ceiling for a much larger, more elastic one -- it is not a Big-O improvement.

drills.q: A candidate implements Course Schedule (cycle detection in a directed graph) using a single boolean 'visited' array: if a DFS call reaches an already-visited node, it reports a cycle. Show a valid, cycle-free dependency graph where this produces a false positive, and explain the fix.
drills.a: Consider A -> B -> D and A -> C -> D (a diamond: D depends on both B and C, which both depend on A). DFS from A visits B, then D (marking D visited), returns, then visits C, which tries to visit D again -- D is already marked visited, so the single-visited-set check incorrectly reports a cycle, even though this graph has no cycle at all. The fix is three states per node: unvisited, in-progress (currently an ancestor on the active DFS call stack), and done (fully explored). A cycle is only real if DFS encounters a node that is currently in-progress (an ancestor calling back to itself); encountering a done node via a second path is normal and expected in a DAG.

drills.q: Design the iterative postorder traversal trick using a preorder-style single stack, and explain why the reversal step produces correct postorder output.
drills.a: Run an iterative traversal that visits root, then pushes LEFT child before RIGHT child (the opposite push order from standard preorder), producing the sequence 'root, right, left' as output. Then reverse that entire output list. Reversing the sequence 'root, right, left' for every subtree recursively yields exactly 'left, right, root', which is the definition of postorder -- the reversal of a root-right-left traversal is mathematically identical to a left-right-root traversal.

drills.q: A candidate's Path Sum II solution appends the current node's value to a shared 'current_path' list on the way down, and at each leaf that matches the target sum, appends 'current_path' (the list object itself, not a copy) directly to the results list. Explain what goes wrong and why.
drills.a: The 'current_path' list continues being mutated (values appended and popped) as the DFS traversal proceeds to explore sibling branches after this leaf's match is recorded. Because all recorded results point to the SAME underlying list object, every one of them ends up reflecting whatever 'current_path' looks like at the very end of the entire traversal (likely empty, since backtracking pops every entry back off by the time DFS fully completes), rather than the specific path that existed at the moment each individual match was found. The fix is to append a shallow copy of current_path (e.g. current_path[:] in Python, or a new list constructed from it) at each match, not the live reference.

drills.q: A JSON-parsing service uses straightforward recursive descent to validate incoming payloads and starts crashing with stack overflow errors after a change allows arbitrarily nested user-submitted objects. Diagnose the failure mode and describe the fix, being precise about what does and doesn't improve.
drills.a: This is the classic deep-nesting-exhausts-the-call-stack failure: a maliciously or accidentally deeply nested JSON payload (a chain of thousands of nested objects/arrays) forces recursion depth proportional to nesting depth, which can exceed the runtime's call-stack limit (a real, exploitable denial-of-service pattern against recursive parsers on untrusted input). The fix is to convert the recursive descent into an iterative traversal using an explicit, heap-allocated stack of pending work items, which moves the O(depth) memory footprint from the small, fixed call stack to the much larger heap. This does not reduce the Big-O space complexity (still O(depth) either way) -- it only replaces a small hard ceiling with a much larger, more forgiving one. A complementary, often necessary fix is also imposing and enforcing an explicit maximum nesting depth and rejecting payloads that exceed it, regardless of which traversal style is used.

drills.q: Compare DFS-postorder-based topological sort with Kahn's BFS-based algorithm: what does each naturally give you 'for free', and how does each detect a cycle?
drills.a: DFS-postorder topological sort: run DFS to completion, recording each node in a postorder list as it finishes, then reverse that list to get a valid topological order; it detects a cycle via the same three-state (unvisited/in-progress/done) mechanism used for directed cycle detection -- encountering an in-progress node during the DFS means a cycle exists. Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove nodes with zero remaining in-degree, decrementing the in-degree of their neighbors, appending removed nodes to the output in removal order; it detects a cycle implicitly, simply by the fact that if a cycle exists, some nodes will never reach zero in-degree and therefore never get removed, so the final output list will be shorter than the total node count. Both are O(V+E); DFS-postorder builds naturally on existing DFS infrastructure and cycle-state tracking, while Kahn's is often considered easier to trace by hand and gives a very direct 'stuck nodes = cycle' signal.
